beats.t: The smell of fried sugar rushed at them as soon as they stepped off the lotus-leaf boat. Singing shops and plates tapping rhythms filled the alley. Yeoni found the food before their nose harder to believe than the mirror trial they had just finished. Hunger was the simplest proof of being alive.
Look at that. They're frying clouds. Actual clouds, and they don't disappear in the oil. Yeongnyangi, skip the explanation. Just tell me if I can eat them.
You can. But when you pay, watch what they take besides money. Especially if the first thing a shop says is that it's free.

A child was playing a small drum in the alley. People clapped, but their expressions vanished when the drumming stopped. Clear fragments piled up before the child instead of coins. In each, someone's smiling lips appeared briefly.
That isn't money. Are they giving away their smiles? The kid is entertaining, but shouldn't someone ask if they get those smiles back afterward?
No business would work if you got them back. The receiver feels good today; the giver gets a full stomach today. That's enough. Calculate tomorrow too, and you'll never buy anything.

The black tiger sat on a red rooftop awning. The ring mark on its forepaw was hidden under the cloak, but river sand still clung to the damp gold trim. Yeoni raised a hoof in greeting. Only after checking the surroundings did the tiger nod.
Is your paw okay? Won't you hurt it again climbing so high? Come down. I can't come rescue you all the way up there right now.
Do you always ask about wounds first when you meet someone again? More interested in what they hurt than what they gained? What an exhausting habit.

The tiger jumped down. An empty plate happened to be beneath it, but slid aside before its paw landed. Yeongnyangi noticed. Yeoni was watching only the child's drumsticks. The child gripped them so tightly that the handles dug into small palms.
Can't you rest? You've been playing the same song over and over. Your hands have been bleeding for a while. Getting applause doesn't have to hurt that much.

The child tried to stop, then resumed drumming. A tag hanging around their neck trembled. Small print on it said they had borrowed today's applause in advance. The line saying they could not leave the stage until it was repaid was on the back.
That child chose it. Rather than a song nobody heard, they wanted an audience even if it meant debt. Grant someone's wish and they always call you the villain afterward.
They wished for applause, not bleeding hands. Did you even give them time to read the back? Showing only the pretty front and calling it a choice is pretty underhanded, isn't it?

The tiger slowly flattened its ears. When Yeongnyangi moved in front of Yeoni, the tiger did not retreat. Instead, it pressed the red jewel at its throat with a paw. The child's drumming broke for a beat, then accelerated.
Don't touch that necklace, Yeoni. Break it by force here and you tear the child's voice, not the drum. Those who write these contracts always use the victim as a shield.
Then we can be the audience. Not borrowed applause—applause from people listening right now. Yeongnyangi, got any rhythm? If not, just match your paws to mine.

Yeoni tried to follow the quick drumbeat and fell twice. Onlookers laughed. They got up and tapped the ground again. Only after giving up on looking skilled could they properly hear the drum. The child always struggled most just before the chorus.
Rest here. I'll take that beat until you come back in. There's no line saying you have to do everything alone. If there is, show it to me now.

Two small hooves tapped the ground. A dull sound to call applause. Yet the child looked up for the first time. Someone was not waiting for the song to end, but stepping inside it to fill an empty space.
Count to three, then breathe. Keep hold of your own beat. If matching other people leaves you breathless, you can rest a moment.

Yeongnyangi's tail tapped the floor. Its slow, precise sound steadied the child's hands. One onlooker followed the same rhythm. Then two, three. The alley's sound gradually changed. Among purchased cheers, newly born applause began to mingle.
Why do they like such a mess? It's wrong. Missed beats, cracked voices. Worse than the arranged performance.
That kid just smiled at us. They know we're matching them. Being good at it can wait. Today, those hands need to rest first.

The tiger looked at the child's tag. The debt engraved on its front was fading stroke by stroke. Not because the borrowed applause had been repaid, but because borrowing was no longer necessary. That form of repayment did not appear in the ledger.

A black droplet sprang from the tiger's paw and struck the tag. The final line binding the child blurred. At the same moment, the tiny name on the tag's edge was sucked into the droplet. The child, catching their breath after setting down the drumsticks, did not see.
You just helped, didn't you? I saw it. Even if you tell me to pretend I didn't, I did. I'm saying thank you. Fold your ears if you don't want to hear it.
You saw what you wanted to see. You can take the child today. But leave the tag. I clear away the paperwork when accounts are settled.

The child broke a fried cloud in half. One half went to Yeoni; the other was placed before the tiger. The tiger looked first at the cut edges, as though measuring which portion was larger. The child smiled again without even looking at the sizes.
There's some for you too. No fine print on the back this time. Taste it. You can get angry if it's bad, though I didn't fry it, so I can't take responsibility.

The tiger took a bite. The child smiled and thanked it, unaware of what had been stolen. The tiger looked from that smile to Yeoni's. It did not take even a single ledger page to make them believe a debt had been erased.
Let's go, Yeoni. Leave someone who needs rest to rest. Keep demanding proof of what you've received, and even gratitude becomes a shackle.

Yeoni left the alley with the child. Yeongnyangi watched the tiger's paws to the last. When the droplet at its feet slipped behind the awning, his violet eyes narrowed. The tiger swallowed the remaining food without avoiding his gaze.
Free them once, and they never see the second line. When will you see it, Yeoni? Could you recognize it without that cat?

The tiger climbed onto the awning and looked down the alley. The shopkeeper who lent applause had vanished. Only the ledger remained. A red mark was stamped inside the cover—the same shape as the marking on the tiger's forehead.

The tiger erased the child's name from the original ledger. Not destroyed it: moved it into the lining of its own cloak. One golden thread turned black. The paw closing the back cover did not tremble. The tag it would show Yeoni tomorrow was clean now.
